name: Blogr
subcategory: AI blog post generation and publishing
tagline: AI tool that drafts SEO-oriented blog posts and pushes them to your site on a schedule.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The writing part is genuinely commodity: a prompt, a model call, a markdown file with frontmatter, done in an afternoon. What you do not get for free is the stuff around it: keyword and SERP data that costs money to license, internal linking across an existing archive, image generation, and one-click publishing into whatever CMS you actually use. A one-shot build handles a static site or a WordPress endpoint fine and falls apart the moment you want Webflow, Shopify, Ghost, and Notion all working. If your goal is volume of mediocre posts, you can absolutely self-host that, and you should ask whether volume of mediocre posts is the goal. Call it a weekend, with the keyword research left as an exercise.
coreLoopDIY: Takes a list of topics or keywords, generates structured blog drafts with an LLM, writes them as markdown with frontmatter, and optionally posts them to WordPress.
requirements: An LLM API key (OpenAI or Anthropic)
A target site: a static site repo, or WordPress with an application password
Your own keyword ideas, since real search volume data is paid
whatYouLose: Keyword and SERP data: you are guessing at topics instead of pulling volume and difficulty numbers
Multi-CMS publishing connectors, so anything beyond your one chosen target is manual
Automatic internal linking and site-wide content planning across an existing archive
Hosted scheduling, so the cron job is your problem and your laptop's uptime
Inline image generation, alt text pipelines, and the small formatting polish that makes drafts publishable
moatNotes: The defensible bits are the CMS connector zoo and licensed search data, not the writing.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because nobody who buys this wants to maintain a publishing pipeline. They want to type a topic, or not even that, and have posts appear on a live site with images and links and a schedule that keeps running when they are asleep. The model call is the cheap part of that sentence; the connectors, the retry logic, the keyword feed, and the dashboard that makes it feel like a system are the expensive parts. A self-hosted script covers the cheap part perfectly and leaves you owning the rest.
notes: Generating blog posts is a weekend script; getting them to appear on six different CMSes with real keyword data behind them is the actual product.
prompt:
Build a local CLI tool called "postmill" that drafts and publishes blog posts.

Stack, no substitutions: TypeScript, Node 20, tsx for running, commander for the CLI, zod for config validation, gray-matter for frontmatter, the OpenAI SDK for generation. No web UI, no database, no accounts, no telemetry.

Layout:
- topics.yaml: a list of entries, each with title or keyword, optional angle, optional target word count.
- content/: generated markdown files, slugified filenames, YAML frontmatter with title, description, slug, date, tags, draft: true.
- postmill.config.yaml: site name, audience, tone, default word count, forbidden phrases list.
- .env for OPENAI_API_KEY and optional WP_URL, WP_USER, WP_APP_PASSWORD. Ship .env.example, gitignore .env.

Commands:
- postmill outline "keyword": prints a proposed H2/H3 outline, does not write a file.
- postmill draft: for each topic in topics.yaml without a matching file in content/, generate an outline, then generate the full post section by section (one model call per section, so long posts do not degrade), then a meta description. Write markdown. Skip anything already drafted unless --force.
- postmill publish FILE: POST to the WordPress REST API at /wp-json/wp/v2/posts using basic auth from .env, status draft by default, --live to publish. Store the returned post id back into the frontmatter so re-publishing updates instead of duplicating.
- postmill list: table of files, titles, word counts, published ids.

Rules: retry model calls twice with backoff, never overwrite a file silently, strip any phrase in the forbidden list and regenerate that section once, write a run log to .postmill/runs.jsonl.

Out of scope, do not build: keyword volume or SERP data, image generation, Webflow/Ghost/Shopify connectors, scheduling (tell me the cron line to add instead), any hosted dashboard.

Finish with a README showing a first run: install, .env setup, three topics in topics.yaml, draft, publish as a WordPress draft.
